column2: The proofs arrive from the printer; the margin around the ball bearing is too wide; Albers refuses and demands that his name be removed if the defect is not corrected; Johnson replies with a contrite letter promising exactly three millimeters. Words: Albers demands the correction or else the removal of his name; Johnson apologizes and confirms the three-millimeter margin. Atmosphere: a perfectionist's tension, wounded dignity Stakes: Bauhaus rigor transplanted to America, down to the millimeter

Leigh encourages Albers to stay on at BMC, arguing that someone with a different technical training is needed; Albers, believing in a misunderstanding due to his English, replies in German for the sake of “directness and simplicity,” proposes a visit to Bennington from April 8 to 15, details his studies at the great German art schools before 1920, and points out that he also paints in oil. Leigh refuses for good: the department already has one member of German background, and someone more essentially American is needed, who knows “the background of our girls”. A letter in German; a visit proposed for April 8-15; Leigh's remark on American experience Consequences: Albers stays at Black Mountain; Albers possibly devastated; the hypothesis of a Eurocentrism on Albers's part toward women, noted by Mrs. Leigh
Albers writes to Kandinsky that the constant stream of visitors almost always attends his classes and above all praises his English, which is nonetheless far from perfect.

Before the end of July 1934, Albers turns up at MoMA with his recent woodcuts, hoping for help in exhibiting them, perhaps at the museum itself. A portfolio of woodcuts brought in person Consequences: Warburg at once writes to Agnes Mongan (Fogg, Harvard) and Charles Sawyer (Addison Gallery); only the Addison accepts

Albers, a year after his arrival, shows up with his portfolio of woodcuts, hoping for an exhibition at the museum; Warburg writes at once to Mongan and Sawyer, pressing them. Words: Warburg: several museums have already asked for this exhibition, reply as soon as possible Atmosphere: The émigré's zeal, the patron's swift generosity Stakes: Making the artist (and not only the teacher) exist in America

Mail takes about two weeks by ship. Mies replies curtly to Johnson's letter of November 2: he refuses to endorse an exhibition of “students” he has not trained and demands the strictest standards. Johnson, offended, replies that he is leaving the Modern and threatens that there will be no more architecture exhibitions in America — a false prediction. Johnson's letter dated November 2; Mies's reply dated November 23; two weeks in the mail Consequences: A temporary break; after the war Johnson again becomes one of Mies's greatest supporters.
Lead editorial by Walter Locke (a friend of Rice's) in the Dayton Daily News (Ohio) on November 16, 1934; article by Grace Alexandra Young, “Art as a Fourth R,” in Arts and Decorations, January 1935.

The Alberses' first entry into Latin America, in Cuba, in the winter of 1934, shortly after their arrival in the United States at the end of 1933. Consequences: The start of a series of more than fourteen trips

The Alberses and their friends Ted and Bobbie Dreier traveled by car and ferry from Miami to Havana; Josef gave three lectures at the Lyceum Club there. They fell under the spell of the Latin world. Palm trees, tropical fruit and flowers, Spanish wine at New Year's, very strong coffee, black tobacco, rum; Josef's letter to the Kandinskys of February 4, 1935 Consequences: The beginning of the Alberses' lasting bond with Latin America

Invited by Clara Porset, Anni and Josef set out with their friends Ted and Bobbie Dreier by car and ferry from Miami to Havana; Josef gives three lectures at the Lyceum Club there. the heat and sun of Cuba, palm trees, abundant tropical fruit and flowers, Spanish wine on New Year's Eve, very strong coffee, black cigarettes, rum Consequences: A first taste of the Latin world, the start of two decades of Latin American travel

Arrival by car and ferry from Miami with the Dreiers; welcomed by Porset; Josef gives three lectures; a dazzled discovery of Cuba, down to the New Year's Eve with Spanish wine Words: Josef to the Kandinskys: everything different from North America, everything excellent Atmosphere: Heat, sun, palm trees, rum and strong coffee Stakes: A first contact with the Latin world, love at first sight

Invited by the Cuban designer Clara Porset, who had passed through Black Mountain in September, Josef gives a three-day series of lectures at the Lyceum in Havana (founded in 1928 as a women's social club, later merged with the Lawn Tennis Club). The Alberses travel with Ted and Bobbie Dreier in the Dreiers' car. The Dreiers' car; the Lyceum founded in 1928 Consequences: The start of the series of Latin American trips

Shortly before a visit from his mother, who has come from the Netherlands, de Kooning rents a temporary space where he and Diaz pass themselves off as husband and wife; his mother sees through the deception, learns of Diaz's abortion, and discovers the existence of Juliet Browner Consequences: Reveals the domineering personality of the mother, who threatened to kill herself if her son crossed her

Anni will report in 1970 that the collection began by chance in 1935; they will call the figures “ídolos,” an almost religious term that Rivera also used. Hundreds of figures and objects, later bequeathed to Yale's Peabody Museum; never displayed at home, kept in cupboards and crates Consequences: The collection bequeathed to the Peabody Museum

Josef Albers photographs the site of Monte Albán, including the ball court; montages of 40 and 39 contact prints preserved at the Foundation. montage “Monte Alban '35” of 40 contact prints on cardboard, 20.6 x 50.8 cm

The collection of pre-Hispanic figures and objects, which Josef and Anni invest with an almost religious meaning by calling them idolos, begins without ceremony in 1935. A selection of the smallest pieces will be published in 1970, with an introduction by Anni; the whole will eventually go to Yale's Peabody Museum. hundreds of pieces; stored in closets and drawers, never displayed; 1970 publication Consequences: Private talismans of true creativity, never shown in the house.

Adamic visits the college for three months in 1935, impressed by its educational and communal character, especially as expressed in the ideas of the founder, John Andrew Rice; he holds there the conversations recounted in his chapter “The Long Road”. Consequences: Publication of “The Long Road” in My America (Harper, 1938), 615-45; article “Education on a Mountain,” Harper's, April 1936

Rice sets out his educational philosophy to Adamic: method over content, process over results, training of the imagination, art as the beginning of education. Consequences: According to the editor, these ideas remained viable and affecting throughout the life of the college

Sly arrives in 1935: about 53 students, a faculty grown to 18-20 members; enough musicians (students, teachers, and wives) for ensemble music. 53 students; 18-20 teachers Consequences: Musical activities expand: ensemble, madrigals, limited tours (a nearby state teachers' college)
Sly arrives at the college: about 53 students, a faculty grown to 18-20 people 53 students, 18-20 teachers Consequences: a boom in musical activities; ensemble music becomes possible

The housewarming of the music cottage (a few upright pianos, a few fireplaces) is celebrated with hot dogs and Coke, or fall cider; Albers came; everyone speared his sausage on an unbent coat hanger, but Albers bent his into an S and set his sausage on it over the fire; it was pointed out to him that a point had its advantages, and he replied that he liked the S shape very much; his sausage fell into the fire hot dogs, Coke or cider, a hanger bent into an S, fireplaces, upright pianos
Norman and Nan marry in 1935 while they are at the college. Consequences: four children; between them they served on more than 20 boards of charitable associations
The psychoanalyst Fritz Moellenhoff, who has known Albers since 1920 in Germany, comes to Black Mountain in 1935 with his wife Anna (also a physician), at Albers's suggestion.
The German psychoanalyst Fritz Moellenhoff and his wife Anna, a physician, arrive under Albers's auspices and stay several years. Consequences: a clinical eye on the student population

Public productions: Gloria Mundi, The Twelve-Pound Look, The Wild Duck, Paul Green's Fixin's. Class productions with no outside audience: The Bear, Heywood Broun's Death Says It Isn't So, an original play, I Died Eight Years Ago, two one-act plays by Lord Dunsany, the prologue of Androcles and the Lion, and passages from Saint Joan and Macbeth.

During his vacation, Wunsch decides that the reality of Black Mountain lies in human relationships; his energy will go into helping people find themselves: he was beginning to see drama as therapy. Consequences: A psychodramatic outlook useful to some students; scorned by Albers as an excuse for mediocrity under the guise of “self-expression”.

Around the mid-thirties, the town votes for prohibition; Roy, the owner of a small beer bar near the station, learns that the student Stephen Forbes comes from a wealthy New England family and proposes that he build a café just outside the town limits. Forbes agrees to finance it anonymously, but the students eventually discover the investment and even its amount — without Forbes understanding how. A small beer bar called Roy's, near the station; Forbes thought he was financing it anonymously Consequences: The birth of Roy's, the college's favorite haunt for conversation

In the third year, the president of Bennington College and his wife spend two days at the college; Rice, who resents the snobbish attitude of Bennington circles when Black Mountain was starting out, stays frigid toward this couple, whom he considers complacent. A two-day stay, the college's third year Consequences: An unsuccessful visit

Fred Mangold, a personal friend of Adams, persuades him to visit Black Mountain in 1935, with the possible idea of joining the faculty to strengthen the sciences. After a week, Adams concludes that the college truly applies the principle that learning begins only when the student wants to learn, but that the existing science courses (Georgia in chemistry, Dreier in physics, Anna Moellenhoff in biology) are poorly attended because the students do not see the need for them; no member of the staff takes a science course, whereas several take drawing, music, literature, history, and languages. He advises against expanding the sciences. a one-week stay Consequences: no scientific expansion recommended

Mangold replies that science is neglected for lack of good teachers, except Mrs. Moellenhoff, who, from the opening of her biology course, has had eight students simply “goofy” about the subject. Adams replies that biology, the science of the living body, naturally appeals more than the other sciences, and that if Black Mountain wants to teach only what the students want to learn, it must not introduce subjects simply because society has certified them as important. eight “goofy” biology students

Two years after the episode of the Black student, the heating broke down in the cottage where the Black staff lived. Anna Moellenhoff insisted that they be given two large rooms in Lee Hall, since several had bad colds. The Black staff refused: Rubye Lipsey explained that it would arouse too much hostility in the village. two large rooms offered in Lee Hall

Albers designs a logo that sweeps away traditional heraldry, a symbol of clarity, sobriety, and modernity: a simple ring, with the college's full address, without monogram or motto. a simple ring, the full address printed Consequences: a 1935 flyer spreads the logo
First visit to Mexico, followed by fourteen trips to Latin and South America fourteen trips in all Consequences: The birth of documentary photographs of ancient architecture and indigenous weaving
After the period of printmaking in Berlin and then in North Carolina, Albers takes up painting in 1935. Consequences: Opens the way for the painted series of the 1930s and 1940s

After his first visit, Dewey writes to Rice that the college's work is imperative for democracy and that it exists at the very “grass roots” of a democratic life. Dewey will visit the college several times, join the advisory council, and give hundreds of books to the library. Consequences: The college legitimized by the major figure of progressive education.

Wunsch joins the college as instructor in English and dramatics, having been Rice's colleague at Rollins College in Florida. title: instructor in English and Dramatics Consequences: Rice's informal seminar turned into a structured creative writing course
Albers publishes in Progressive Education (vol. 12, p. 391) an article in English, written during his first years at Black Mountain, asserting that rules arise from experience and come afterward.

The start of frequent trips to Mexico, where the two artists discover the ancient arts of the Americas, which leave a deep mark on their work. Consequences: Pre-Columbian influences in both bodies of work.

Shortly after the purchase, Anni shows her piece to the renowned archaeologist George C. Vaillant, who confirms that it is an authentic little Mexican treasure; from then on the couple takes a passionate interest in Mexican culture. Consequences: Thirteen more trips to Mexico

In the 1930s, the art historian Meyer Schapiro criticizes Fuller's shelters for their naïveté: believing that better housing controlled by capitalist corporations will transform the structure of capitalism is an illusion, since these firms are party to overproduction, competition, and speculative layoffs. Consequences: A lasting critique of “revolution by design”
Albers's lecture on abstract art in Asheville.

In the mid-1930s, shortly after his arrival in America, Albers designs for Rena Rosenthal's shop an upholstery fabric of synthetic fibers, then a screen fabric of cut cellulose cotton and rayon, in unusual pastels, which allows one to see out without being seen. cut cellulose cotton, rayon, horizontal stripes of pastels
Allan Sly and Dante Fiorillo join the music faculty; Fiorillo is appointed composer in residence, supported by a Guggenheim fellowship.

Coming from Bennington in 1935, aiming at a major in art: half her courses in drawing, color, and art studies, the other half in German, French literature, music, world economics, and Plato with Rice. In the senior division, she drops from six to five courses a semester for her final project and exam review. six, then five courses a semester

A stay of nearly two months suggested by Henry Allen Moe. Adamic is enchanted by the place and the people, especially Rice; the two become friends at once, and Rice develops his ideas and experiences for the article Adamic decides to write for Harper's. Length: nearly two months Consequences: The article “Education on a Mountain”

De Kooning is accepted into the Federal Art Project, launched by Roosevelt to provide commissions for artists hit by the Depression. The program will produce more than 2,500 murals, 18,000 sculptures, and hundreds of thousands of prints, paintings, and photographs across America. 2,500 murals; 18,000 sculptures; a salary judged rather decent, allowing one to live modestly but well during the Depression Consequences: For the first time de Kooning can devote himself entirely to his art; a decisive experience.

The WPA's Federal Art Project is launched in 1935 to relieve poverty; Burckhardt remembers that “Bill” was on it for a year or more — the “$23.50 Club,” named after the weekly allowance. $23.50 a week
Rudy Burckhardt and Edwin Denby (poet and dance critic) are de Kooning's neighbors across the landing on West 21st Street and become his first committed collectors.
Photograph of Anni Albers in the Dreiers' car, taken by Josef Albers (caption).

In the mid-1930s, Josef Albers is part of a group of artists demonstrating in front of MoMA to protest the lack of attention to purely abstract artists; he believes Barr never forgave him for it. Consequences: Alfred Barr's lasting grudge against Josef Albers

First steady income through the Federal Art Project; he astonishes his fellow artists by the share of his salary spent on materials and art books. Whole tubes squeezed onto the palette for an hour's work; paintings reworked for years, scraped with a razor at the end of the day

Exhibition of Albers's prints during the month of January 1935; Sawyer had probably seen the prints in Warburg's office in early September 1934. The Addison's first exhibition devoted to a single European modernist artist. Fifteen works shown according to the checklist, out of a larger group; Boston and local newspapers published brief notices but no reviews Consequences: Sawyer will continue to support Albers with exhibition opportunities in the following years

The housewarming of the music cottage around the fire; everyone spears his sausage on an unbent coat hanger; Albers bends his into an S and lays his sausage on it; the advantage of the point is explained to him; he refuses; the sausage falls into the fire Words: “I like very much the S-form” Atmosphere: the warmth of the fire, the smell of sausages, Coke or fall cider Stakes: Albers's stubborn genius, down to a makeshift grill

Adamic, seeking a pastoral escape from New York, is given a guest room and an invitation to dinner; the table brings together faculty and students who serve one another; the conversation goes on very late into the night; he stays two and a half months instead of a few days Words: Table conversation, its content not reported, that went on past midnight Atmosphere: Communal warmth, nighttime intellectual ferment Stakes: The hurried visitor becomes a long-staying guest: the birth of the account that will launch the myth

The philosopher's first visit; he observes the community, then writes Rice a letter of support. Words: The college exists at the very roots of a democratic life; its work is imperative whatever happens in the present crisis. Stakes: The endorsement of the greatest American educator.

While Josef and the Dreiers visit the inside of a church, Anni waits in the car; a little boy comes up with a young goat under his arm and offers to sell the animal or a small figurine head wrapped in a handkerchief; Anni buys the head for a few pesos. Words: The boy offers the kid or the figurine; Anni will later say that she would not have imagined such a piece was still to be had Atmosphere: The heat of the Mexican road, chance, enchantment Stakes: The chance birth of a collection that will unite the couple for fifty years

Three months after his arrival, exhausted and full of doubt, Wunsch asks for a private talk; Rice takes him to his room, listens to him, suggests that he is tired and judges only by tangible results, and proposes a vacation. Rice suggests a trip to the Kentucky Derby. Consequences: Wunsch goes on vacation and redefines his role.

Wunsch is perhaps expecting the sledgehammer; Rice takes him to his room, listens to him, finds him tired, and suggests a vacation — a trip to the Kentucky Derby, for instance. Words: Rice judges that Wunsch measures his work only by its tangible results. Atmosphere: Warm, calm, with Rice's whimsy. Stakes: Wunsch expected to be crushed; he is cared for.

Mangold, in charge of the summer sessions, complains of “nincompoops” (letter to Rice of July 9, 1935), predicts the death of the college (June 19, 1935), speaks of castration (to Bailey, August 28, 1935), then, from Mexico on June 26, 1936, warns his successor: pray that no Adventist desecrates the woods with vegetarian orgies; last year's crop was an abomination, apart from a few lecherous barbarians who added a picturesque note — the novelty lay in the beards.

An article developing a space-time folded into parallel sheets joined by a bridge, using only general relativity and Maxwell's equations — the first description of a wormhole. Physical Review 48 (1), p. 73 Consequences: The concept taken up by Wheeler and Fuller (1962, instability), Hjellming (1971), Thorne and Morris (1988).
Joins the Federal Art Project; a mural for the Williamsburg Federal Housing Project never carried out; leaves the WPA after a year for lack of American citizenship

Knickerbocker, in his late thirties, arrives highly recommended by his teachers at Harvard, where he is finishing a doctorate in psychology specializing in children's problems; he and his wife ran a small school for disturbed children. Two of the three recommending professors stress his “unusual independence”. Consequences: From his arrival he voices his doubts about Rice's classroom tactics, which in his view produce fear and break people without rebuilding them

Katherine Dreier (who had visited the Berlin Bauhaus in 1933 and knew Albers through her nephew Theodore and his wife Bobbie) brings an exhibition of her collection to BMC. Works by Archipenko, Burliuk, Campendonk, Gleizes, Kandinsky, Klee, Léger, Miró, Mondrian, Schwitters; the students chose 30-40 paintings from the storeroom to hang in their rooms Consequences: A unique experience: living with the works, seeing them in every light

Dreier opens her storeroom to the residents; each chooses works from among thirty or forty, hangs them in his room, and lives with them day to day. Words: Bobbie Dreier: one could look at them in every light, not just walk past them as in an exhibition; she chose for herself Atmosphere: A rare intimacy with modern masterpieces deep in the North Carolina mountains Stakes: European modernism enters American domestic life

Visiting sites and museums, the Alberses examine ceramic fragments — delicately modeled heads, often broken figurines — found by peasants while plowing; they begin to buy and collect, eventually more than a thousand objects Atmosphere: Incredulous wonder: centuries-old pieces in their hands Stakes: The birth of a collection and a permanent source of inspiration

After two months she feels that something is missing: boys; she hates being made to jump from one subject to another. Consequences: A chance meeting with a former classmate, who suggests the Leonardo da Vinci Art School.

Admitted on the strength of drawings of sculptures, she studies there with Conrad Marca-Relli and becomes friends with the young Milton Resnick. A school founded in 1923 by the sculptor Onorio Ruotolo to offer free instruction to the poor; entirely free when Elaine arrived, the teachers unpaid. Classes in fresco, mural painting, easel painting, drawing, cartooning; nude models — “this is living!”. Consequences: The start of her true vocation.

An active opponent of the U.S.-backed right-wing regime of President Mendieta, Porset went into exile in Mexico and married the artist Xavier Guerrero, close to Diego Rivera's first murals. Consequences: The Guerreros become the Alberses' main link with Mexican artists

The start of the series of trips to Mexico, fourteen in all, some lasting three months. 14 trips in all; some lasting three months Consequences: The start of the collection of pre-Columbian art and of a lasting influence on the Alberses' work

Back in the United States, Albers begins to paint instead of continuing the colored-glass pictures of his Bauhaus years; Mexican themes appear in his painting immediately after the first trip. Consequences: The birth of motifs such as Tenayuca and, later, the series “Homenaje al cuadrado”.

An active opponent of the pro-American right-wing government of President Mendieta, Porset settles in Mexico and marries the artist Xavier Guerrero, who had collaborated on Diego Rivera's first murals; the couple is at the center of a circle of artists engaged in the post-revolutionary fervor. Consequences: The Guerreros become an essential link between the Alberses and Mexican artists, architects, and intellectuals; Porset may have played a part in organizing the August 1936 exhibition

Three months in Mexico; Josef writes that Mexico is the promised land of abstract art, thousands of years old, and measures his progress by his well-being and his output. 7 pounds gained (about 3 kg), 11 oil paintings; “we hope to return soon and often” Consequences: A recurring theme in his correspondence: Mexico feeds his creativity.

After their first Mexican summer, Anni makes two large-format wall hangings, more spontaneous and personal than her Bauhaus works; for the first time she gives titles to her work and signs Monte Alban with the initials “AA” embroidered at lower left — a break with the creative anonymity of the Bauhaus. Monte Alban: a limited palette of blacks, grays, and creamy whites; white weft threads floating on the surface, doubled and shadowed by black wefts evoking the unexcavated mounds Consequences: Goes beyond the orderly geometries of the Bauhaus wall hangings of the late 1920s.

By 1936 at the latest, the Alberses are gathering fragments of pre-Columbian pottery and figurines; little boys offer them through the car window, just as turkeys and goats were sold by the roadside. pottery fragments, finely modeled heads, figurines usually broken, found by peasants plowing their fields; turkeys and goats held out for sale Consequences: the start of a collection and a lasting passion

After his first stay in Mexico, Josef Albers paints Archaeologic I, Archaeologic II, and Temple, now lost and known only from black-and-white photographs. Small paintings, very bright colors according to Irving Finkelstein, who saw them in 1965; concentric compositions evoking archaeological sites Consequences: A possible genesis of the Homage to the Square in the geometric plans of pre-Hispanic stepped temples

Every evening around 11 p.m., the author and the Adamics walked to the nearest newsstand for the morning paper; heated discussions almost daily. One night, during the abdication crisis of Edward VIII, Louis, a stammerer who refused to stammer, ground his teeth at the king (“the damned fool”); the author said he envied a man capable of loving so much, Stella agreed, and Louis retorted with biting courtesy. leaving around 11 p.m. for the morning paper; Louis Adamic, a stammerer who forces the words out

Adamic's article (first in Harper's) prompts inquiries; more applications also arrive thanks to a favorable column by Gaynor Maddox reaching two million readers. After a stormy discussion, it is decided not to enclose reprints of the article with the catalog: too self-congratulatory, contrary to the college's policy of discretion about publicity. Consequences: Applications increase

Elaine shares a studio with her boyfriend Milton Resnick and Ernestine Blumberg (who can sign leases because she has a job); they organize their work spaces and share meals and social life. Consequences: a bohemian milieu: poverty cheerfully scorned, hard work, and conversation

Robert Jonas, an instructor at the Leonardo da Vinci, takes her to an exhibition of the American Abstract Artists and tells her that the two best American artists — de Kooning and Arshile Gorky — are not in it; within two weeks, Elaine has met de Kooning and knows she will marry him. She is under twenty, he is thirty-four; she is still Milton Resnick's girlfriend. “it took me about two weeks”; age gap: she ~20, he 34 Consequences: the start of the relationship that will define her whole life as an artist
A cafeteria companion reports that Bill, madly in love with Elaine, said he wanted to be monogamous for the first time — “just Elaine”.

A painting by Bill appears in the exhibition New Horizons in America at MoMA, alongside Bolotowsky, Browne, Davis, Gorky, Greene, Matulka, and McNeil; Elaine proudly boasts of it to her friends as proof that Bill is a great talent exhibition “New Horizons in America”; artists shown: Ilya Bolotowsky, Byron Browne, Stuart Davis, Arshile Gorky, Balcomb Greene, Jan Matulka, George McNeil Consequences: official confirmation of Elaine's conviction that Bill is a major artist

After a few years, Anni sets up a weaving workshop and begins working and teaching alongside Josef. She directs the weaving program throughout her time there (1933-1948) and makes some of her most ambitious works there. Consequences: Weaving becomes a major discipline at the college.

From 1936 on, Schawinsky conceives his course Stage Studies as a laboratory in which students build an understanding of the fundamentals of stage creation, applying the experimental logic of Albers, whom he admires. The course is listed in the art catalog, separate from Robert Wunsch's Dramatics curriculum. Consequences: Leads to the public performance Spectodrama

A public performance in four parts crowning the Stage Studies course, encompassing optics, form and color, acoustics, sound, language, music, time, space, architecture, technology, and illusion. The neologism Spectodrama combines the Latin specto (I observe) and drama (play), merging spectator and performer, the stage treated as a total work of art. Part 1, scene 7: two figures of movable planes in contrasting colors manipulated to show the variation in color intensity when they overlap; lighting reinforcing the effects

Daily physical work (1-4 p.m.) officially becomes the work program: maintenance of heating and plumbing supervised by Bascomb Allen, roads directed by Josef Albers, cooking guided by the cooks Jack and Rubye Lipsey. work from 1 to 4 p.m.; digging furrows, harvesting corn, repairing showers, maintaining roads Consequences: The college survives the lean years of the Depression thanks to this program, which flattens the hierarchies between teachers and students.

Several women arrive as companions of their partners or in subordinate posts: Irene Schawinsky, tutor in costume design (1936-1938), making the costumes for her husband Xanti's plays; Johanna Jalowetz teaches singing and bookbinding after the death of her husband Heinrich, the campus musicologist. Frankenthaler, Elaine de Kooning, Knight Lawrence, Newhall, and Fiore receive no appointment. Consequences: Some later obtain independent teaching posts; others contribute as students or volunteer teachers.

Rice's writing seminar takes the name “creative writing” in 1936, marking the shift from a tool of progressive education to an art that can be taught alongside music, theater, and the fine arts. Consequences: Techniques and exercises from Wunsch's manual, Studies in Creative Writing (1933), are introduced

Wunsch introduces creative writing at the college, insisting on the “discipline” of writing and conceding that in the end only technique can be taught. Consequences: Creative writing becomes a central element of arts education at Black Mountain.
His sister Janet is born; at sixteen she will be elected Louisiana's yam queen. Louisiana's “Yam-Königin”
Anni uses a “floating” white thread to create a pattern evoking the mysterious authority of ancient inscriptions — textile as text. floating white thread
In the spirit of his idol Herman Melville, Olson ships out for three weeks on a fishing schooner in the summer of 1936. three weeks at sea

Brickmakers unearth quantities of vessels and figurines of surprising variety and refinement, in a style distinct from anything known; once their value is known, systematic looting begins. Consequences: Massive looting of the site; the birth of Tlatilco collecting (including the future Albers collection)

Perry, 65, a former long-distance (cross-country) runner, sets out his reading of Ecclesiastes: putting one's trust in works — pleasures, great achievements, wisdom — is idolatry and vanity; one must act according to one's strength (to every thing a season) without putting one's trust in it; trust goes to God. The reporter agrees, citing the saying that the race is not to the swift. Perry then has doubts: is one career as good as another? The reporter replies that everything looks solid from a distance and crumbles as soon as one takes it in hand. Perry is 65; quotations from Ecclesiastes, ch. IX; the man on the verge of tears Consequences: Mrs. Westover suggests that her husband was perhaps right to stick to one thing

Coming out of a birch thicket, Perry reaches the white fence along Route 4W; a green roadster goes by at 80 miles an hour. He sits down to catch his breath, stares at a broken spark plug on the pavement, and knows that by staring long enough he can bring back to life, in a timeless vision, the whole history of the place (steamrollers, blasts of dynamite, the peddler's horse). Before signs (Gaskell 2½ mi, Middleton 10, Malory 15, Cicero 125), he imagines milestones of time: 5 years, 50 years, 150,000 years. a spark plug with broken porcelain; an old shoe hanging from the sign, worn by rain and sun; a green roadster at 80 mph

Early October: four kids are playing hooky, have lit a fire, are telling dirty stories, and are playing cat's cradle. Perry bursts out of a scarlet thicket, his white figure appearing and disappearing between the trunks; the children point him out with fear and admiration, unable to point because of the strings between their fingers. a fire among the colored trees; string passed from fingers to fingers; Perry's white figure

First billboard: a sexy bare-chested pirate carrying off a smiling girl in a nightgown, captioned “Nature in the Raw is Seldom Mild,” Lucky Strikes, “It's Toasted!”. Second: a bespectacled farmer reading his wife a letter from their son, “just bought a Ford V-8,” “Consult your local Ford dealer”. Third, a Christmas one: a mother in a mauve dress, blond marcelled hair, a faint halo, a baby with the features of the child film star Baby Kelly, two golden candles, Sheffield Farms wishing you a “Merry Xmas”. Fourth: “BUY REM” (cough syrup). Behind them, one showed a girl in tears for not having rented a telephone from Bell. advertisements: Lucky Strikes, Ford V-8, Sheffield Farms, REM, Bell Telephone, Burma Shave (rhymes quoted)

After a year as a full-time artist on the WPA, de Kooning gives up the safer idea of earning his living in the applied arts (commercial illustration) and styles himself a pure artist, fulfilling his adolescent dream. One year on the WPA; he puts, in his own metaphor, all his eggs in the basket of art Consequences: The birth of his path as an independent artist, in doubt and a leap of faith

Becomes close to the first American collectors of his work, Burckhardt and Denby; paints full time, begins the series of standing and seated men; meets the critic Harold Rosenberg. Self Portrait with Imaginary Brother, c. 1938.

A series of linear geometric drawings signed and dated 1936 (PLATES 100-108), the first expression of linear concerns that will later underlie series of prints, engravings on vinyl, and architectural commissions. Seven drawings of the PLATE 100 type, all 1936, with diagonal symmetry (identical when turned 180 degrees), made up of nine to twelve lines, some varied by dotting or thickening; executed with pen and ruler, fine black unmodulated lines; signature and date in light pencil at lower right; one made up of eleven lines of equal thickness in three sizes; two others (PLATES 107-108) completely asymmetrical, more unfinished; one (PLATE 109) made of two continuous lines of constant width. Consequences: These drawings herald the linear work of Albers's next forty years.

Albers and Bolotowsky are founding members of the American Abstract Artists (AAA); Bolotowsky explains that most of the group started from nature to extract its essence, whereas a few, himself among them, began abstract and rejected nature
